Key Findings

  • [ALPHA] observed diversity differs significantly between groups (Kruskal-Wallis, adj. p = 0.0001).
  • [ALPHA] shannon diversity differs significantly between groups (Kruskal-Wallis, adj. p = 0.0001).
  • [ALPHA] simpson diversity differs significantly between groups (Kruskal-Wallis, adj. p = 0.0001).
  • [BETA] Community composition differs significantly between groups by bray_curtis (PERMANOVA: F=14.097, R²=0.196, p=0.0010, permutations within location). PERMDISP p=0.0040 — group dispersions differ, so part of the PERMANOVA signal may reflect spread rather than a shift in composition.
  • [BETA] Community composition differs significantly between groups by jaccard (PERMANOVA: F=6.520, R²=0.101, p=0.0010, permutations within location). PERMDISP p=0.0040 — group dispersions differ, so part of the PERMANOVA signal may reflect spread rather than a shift in composition.
  • [TAXONOMY] Dominant genusa by mean relative abundance: Segatella (32.1%), Bacteroides (15.6%), Phocaeicola (8.3%).
  • [DIFF_ABUND] 18/51 genus taxa differ significantly in CRC_vs_Healthy. Top: Agathobacter, Mediterraneibacter, Megasphaera. 17 are also significant in the sensitivity method with the same direction.
  • [DIFF_ABUND] 20/65 species taxa differ significantly in CRC_vs_Healthy. Top: Roseburia faecis, Agathobacter rectalis, Parabacteroides distasonis. 17 are also significant in the sensitivity method with the same direction.

Statistical Methods

⚠️ Statistical significance does not imply biological causality. Effect sizes and confidence intervals should be considered alongside p-values.
AnalysisMethod Description
Alpha DiversityKruskal-Wallis H-test (non-parametric, k-group comparison on alpha diversity metrics). Effect sizes not applicable for H-test; group means reported.
Beta DiversityPERMANOVA (adonis) with Bray-Curtis and Jaccard dissimilarities. P-values from permutation (n=999). Partial R² reported as effect size.
Differential AbundanceCLR-LM (Centered Log-Ratio Linear Model): Applies CLR transformation then fits a linear model per taxon. Compositionally valid but does not include explicit bias correction. Multiple testing corrected by Benjamini-Hochberg FDR.
Multiple TestingCorrection method: fdr_bh (Benjamini-Hochberg FDR by default). Significance threshold α = 0.05.
FunctionalWilcoxon rank-sum test on HUMAnN3 pathway abundances per group, with FDR correction.

Biological Interpretation

⚠️ Important: The following interpretations are based solely on statistically supported observations. Associations between microbial taxa and phenotypes are correlational — they do not establish causation. Biological interpretation of microbiome data requires experimental validation and domain expertise.

Statistically Supported Observations

  • [ALPHA] observed diversity differs significantly between groups (Kruskal-Wallis, adj. p = 0.0001).
  • [ALPHA] shannon diversity differs significantly between groups (Kruskal-Wallis, adj. p = 0.0001).
  • [ALPHA] simpson diversity differs significantly between groups (Kruskal-Wallis, adj. p = 0.0001).
  • [BETA] Community composition differs significantly between groups by bray_curtis (PERMANOVA: F=14.097, R²=0.196, p=0.0010, permutations within location). PERMDISP p=0.0040 — group dispersions differ, so part of the PERMANOVA signal may reflect spread rather than a shift in composition.
  • [BETA] Community composition differs significantly between groups by jaccard (PERMANOVA: F=6.520, R²=0.101, p=0.0010, permutations within location). PERMDISP p=0.0040 — group dispersions differ, so part of the PERMANOVA signal may reflect spread rather than a shift in composition.
  • [TAXONOMY] Dominant genusa by mean relative abundance: Segatella (32.1%), Bacteroides (15.6%), Phocaeicola (8.3%).
  • [DIFF_ABUND] 18/51 genus taxa differ significantly in CRC_vs_Healthy. Top: Agathobacter, Mediterraneibacter, Megasphaera. 17 are also significant in the sensitivity method with the same direction.
  • [DIFF_ABUND] 20/65 species taxa differ significantly in CRC_vs_Healthy. Top: Roseburia faecis, Agathobacter rectalis, Parabacteroides distasonis. 17 are also significant in the sensitivity method with the same direction.

Note on Compositional Data

Microbiome abundance data is inherently compositional (relative, not absolute). Apparent differences in one taxon's relative abundance may reflect changes in other taxa. CLR-based tests compare each taxon to the sample's geometric mean; they do not recover changes in absolute abundance.

Limitations

  • Group is fully confounded with sequencing batch: all 30 CRC samples come from BioProject PRJNA531273 and all 30 healthy controls from PRJNA397112 (a separate, earlier cohort). Any CRC-vs-healthy difference can also reflect differences in sample collection, DNA extraction, library preparation or sequencing run. This cannot be corrected statistically in this design.
  • Different read pre-processing between projects: fastp removed almost no CRC reads but ~8% of healthy-control reads, indicating the two projects' FASTQ files differ in quality or prior trimming.
  • Shallow subset: only the first 100,000 SRA spots per sample were analysed (not a random subsample), far below the original sequencing depth; rare taxa and low-abundance differences are underpowered.
  • No host-read removal: the human reference index was not available, so human reads remain in the input; they are mostly unclassified or assigned to Homo sapiens by Kraken2 and do not enter the bacterial relative abundances, but they reduce effective depth.
  • No functional profiling: HUMAnN3 was not run (database does not fit on disk; depth too low for reliable pathway estimates).
  • Short-read metagenomics: Species-level resolution may be limited for closely related organisms. Strain-level information is generally not recoverable.
  • Database dependency: Taxonomic classification is limited to organisms represented in the Kraken2 database. Novel or poorly characterized taxa will be unclassified.
  • Relative abundance: Metagenomics generates compositional data. Absolute microbial loads require spike-in standards or independent quantification.
  • Sample size: Statistical power for differential analysis depends on sample size. Small cohorts may have insufficient power to detect modest effect sizes.
  • Host contamination: Residual host reads may affect downstream analysis if host removal was not performed or if the reference genome was incomplete.
  • Confounders: Technical batch effects, DNA extraction methods, and library preparation can influence results and should be considered in study design.
